# Cryptographic Building Blocks

This appendix introduces the primitives the rest of the book takes for
granted. It is written for a reader who knows what a hash function does and
that public-key cryptography involves a key pair, but who has not studied
cryptography. Each section says what the primitive promises, what it does
not promise, which concrete algorithms FOKS uses, and where to read more.
Only primitives that actually appear in `foks-rs` are included.

## Hash functions

A cryptographic hash function maps an input of any length to a fixed-size
*digest*. Three properties are expected. *Preimage resistance*: given a
digest, it is infeasible to find any input that produces it. *Second
preimage resistance*: given an input, it is infeasible to find a different
input with the same digest. *Collision resistance*: it is infeasible to find
any two inputs with the same digest.

Collision resistance is the property most protocols lean on, because it is
what lets a digest stand in for the data. If a chain link commits to the
digest of its predecessor, collision resistance is what guarantees that
there is only one predecessor it could mean. A 256-bit digest gives 128 bits
of collision resistance (by the birthday bound, an attacker needs about
$2^{128}$ evaluations), which is the accepted security level for the
foreseeable future.

FOKS uses two hash functions.

- **SHA-512/256** (FIPS 180-4) is SHA-512 with a different initial value and
  the output truncated to 256 bits. It has the same 256-bit security as
  SHA-256 but, because only half of its 512-bit internal state is output,
  it is immune to *length-extension*: given $H(m)$ alone, an attacker cannot
  compute the digest of a longer message that begins with $m$, which SHA-256
  permits. It is the hash for every typed hash, HMAC and commitment in the
  protocol.
- **SHA3-256** (FIPS 202) is a member of the Keccak family, built on a
  different design (a sponge over a permutation) from the SHA-2 family. FOKS
  uses it in exactly one place, the hybrid key combiner
  (Chapter 4). The choice is inherited from the Go implementation; a side
  effect is that the combiner does not share a failure mode with the hash
  used everywhere else.

References:

- National Institute of Standards and Technology, *Secure Hash Standard (SHS)*, FIPS 180-4, 2015, https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.FIPS.180-4
- National Institute of Standards and Technology, *SHA-3 Standard: Permutation-Based Hash and Extendable-Output Functions*, FIPS 202, 2015, https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.FIPS.202

## Message authentication codes and HMAC

A *message authentication code* (MAC) is a function of a secret key and a
message that produces a short *tag*. Anyone with the key can compute the
tag; nobody without the key can produce a valid tag for a new message, even
after seeing tags on many other messages. A MAC gives *integrity* and
*authenticity* between parties who share a key. It does not give secrecy
and it does not give non-repudiation: either party could have produced the
tag.

HMAC (RFC 2104) is the standard way to build a MAC from a hash function. It
hashes the message twice with the key mixed in at each stage,
$\text{HMAC}(k, m) = H((k \oplus \text{opad}) \| H((k \oplus \text{ipad}) \| m))$,
which avoids the length-extension problem of naive $H(k \| m)$ and has a
proof of security under mild assumptions on $H$. HMAC is also a good
*pseudorandom function*, which is why it doubles as a key-derivation
primitive (below).

FOKS uses HMAC-SHA-512/256 for key derivation, for the integrity bindings
of the key-value store, for name commitments, for capability tokens, and
for the pairing-code key derivation. Tags are verified in constant time so
that a comparison's running time does not reveal how many bytes matched.

References:

- H. Krawczyk, M. Bellare, R. Canetti, *HMAC: Keyed-Hashing for Message Authentication*, RFC 2104, IETF, 1997, https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2104
- M. Bellare, R. Canetti, H. Krawczyk, *Keying Hash Functions for Message Authentication*, CRYPTO 1996, https://cseweb.ucsd.edu/~mihir/papers/kmd5.pdf

## Symmetric authenticated encryption

A symmetric cipher encrypts and decrypts with the same key. Modern practice
always pairs encryption with authentication, so that a modified ciphertext
is rejected rather than decrypted to garbage: this is *authenticated
encryption* (AE). A scheme that also authenticates unencrypted context is
*authenticated encryption with associated data* (AEAD); Chapter 8 explains
the associated-data idea.

Both schemes FOKS uses are built the same way: a *stream cipher* generates
a keystream from the key and a *nonce*, the plaintext is XORed with the
keystream, and a one-time MAC (Poly1305) keyed from the same keystream
produces a 16-byte tag over the ciphertext. The nonce must never repeat
under the same key; if it does, the two keystreams are identical and the
XOR of the two plaintexts leaks, and the tag key repeats, which allows
forgery.

- **XSalsa20-Poly1305** is NaCl's `crypto_secretbox`. Salsa20 has a 64-bit
  nonce, too short to choose at random; XSalsa20 (Bernstein, 2011) extends
  it to 192 bits by first running a hash-like function, HSalsa20, over the
  key and the first 128 nonce bits to produce a subkey. With a 24-byte
  nonce, random nonces are safe. FOKS uses it for every protocol-level
  symmetric encryption: boxed seeds, seed chains, pairing packets. It has
  no associated-data input, so FOKS puts context into the nonce and the
  plaintext.
- **XChaCha20-Poly1305** is the same extended-nonce construction applied to
  ChaCha20 (RFC 8439), Salsa20's successor, with associated data. FOKS uses
  it for local storage only (Chapter 8).

A useful mental model: the cipher provides secrecy against anyone without
the key, the tag provides integrity against anyone without the key, and the
nonce's job is to make each encryption under one key independent of the
others.

References:

- D. J. Bernstein, *Cryptography in NaCl*, 2009, https://cr.yp.to/highspeed/naclcrypto-20090310.pdf
- D. J. Bernstein, *Extending the Salsa20 nonce*, 2011, https://cr.yp.to/snuffle/xsalsa-20110204.pdf
- Y. Nir, A. Langley, *ChaCha20 and Poly1305 for IETF Protocols*, RFC 8439, IETF, 2018, https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8439
- P. Rogaway, *Authenticated-Encryption with Associated-Data*, ACM CCS, 2002, https://web.cs.ucdavis.edu/~rogaway/papers/ad.pdf

## Digital signatures

A signature scheme has a private *signing key* and a public *verify key*.
The signer produces a signature over a message; anyone with the verify key
can check it; nobody without the signing key can produce a valid signature
on a new message. Unlike a MAC, a signature can be verified by parties who
cannot forge it, so it supports public verifiability and non-repudiation.
Signatures are what make FOKS's chains (Part III) checkable by everyone
without trusting the server.

- **Ed25519** (RFC 8032) is the Edwards-curve Digital Signature Algorithm
  over Curve25519. Keys are 32 bytes, signatures 64 bytes, signing is
  deterministic (no per-signature randomness to get wrong), and
  implementations are fast and constant-time. FOKS uses it for every
  software key. The Rust code calls `verify_strict`, which rejects the
  edge-case signatures (small-order components, non-canonical encodings)
  that some verifiers accept.
- **ECDSA over P-256** (FIPS 186-5) is the signature scheme available on PIV
  hardware. It signs a 32-byte digest supplied by the host, so FOKS hashes
  the typed message with SHA-512/256 first. ECDSA is *malleable* (Chapter 7)
  and, unlike Ed25519, requires a fresh random or derived nonce per
  signature; the card handles that internally.

A signature is over bytes, not over meaning. Chapter 3 explains why FOKS
prefixes every signed message with a type ID, and Chapter 9 why the bytes
must have exactly one canonical form.

References:

- S. Josefsson, I. Liusvaara, *Edwards-Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (EdDSA)*, RFC 8032, IETF, 2017, https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8032
- D. J. Bernstein, N. Duif, T. Lange, P. Schwabe, B.-Y. Yang, *High-speed high-security signatures*, Journal of Cryptographic Engineering 2(2), 2012, https://ed25519.cr.yp.to/ed25519-20110926.pdf
- K. Chalkias, F. Garillot, V. Nikolaenko, *Taming the Many EdDSAs*, Security Standardisation Research (SSR), 2020, https://eprint.iacr.org/2020/1244
- National Institute of Standards and Technology, *Digital Signature Standard (DSS)*, FIPS 186-5, 2023, https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.FIPS.186-5

## Diffie-Hellman key agreement

Diffie-Hellman lets two parties who each have a key pair compute a shared
secret that nobody else can compute, without sending the secret. Each
party combines its own private key with the other's public key, and the
mathematics of the group guarantees that both arrive at the same value. If
both keys are long-term (*static-static* DH), the shared secret also
implicitly authenticates the parties: only the two key holders could have
computed it. This is how NaCl's `crypto_box`, and FOKS's hybrid box, know
who sent a message without a signature.

- **X25519** (RFC 7748) is Diffie-Hellman over Curve25519 using only the
  x-coordinate. Keys and shared secrets are 32 bytes. It is designed so
  that any 32-byte string is a valid private key and any 32-byte string can
  be used as a public key without validation, which removes a class of
  implementation errors.
- **P-256 ECDH** is Diffie-Hellman over the NIST P-256 curve, the curve PIV
  cards support. Public keys are points, transmitted in SEC 1 compressed
  form (33 bytes); the shared secret is the x-coordinate of the result
  (32 bytes).

A shared secret from Diffie-Hellman is a group element, not a uniformly
random key, and should be passed through a hash or key-derivation function
before use. NaCl does this with HSalsa20; FOKS's hybrid combiner does it
with SHA3-256.

References:

- W. Diffie, M. Hellman, *New Directions in Cryptography*, IEEE Transactions on Information Theory 22(6), 1976, https://doi.org/10.1109/TIT.1976.1055638
- A. Langley, M. Hamburg, S. Turner, *Elliptic Curves for Security*, RFC 7748, IETF, 2016, https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7748
- D. J. Bernstein, *Curve25519: new Diffie-Hellman speed records*, PKC 2006, https://cr.yp.to/ecdh/curve25519-20060209.pdf
- Certicom Research, *SEC 1: Elliptic Curve Cryptography*, Version 2.0, 2009, https://www.secg.org/sec1-v2.pdf

## Key encapsulation and ML-KEM

A *key encapsulation mechanism* (KEM) is a public-key primitive shaped for
sending a symmetric key. `Encaps(pk)` produces a random shared secret and a
ciphertext; `Decaps(sk, ciphertext)` recovers the shared secret. Unlike
Diffie-Hellman, a KEM is one-directional: the sender needs no key pair of
its own, and the ciphertext carries no information about who sent it. That
is why FOKS pairs ML-KEM with Diffie-Hellman rather than replacing it.

**ML-KEM** (FIPS 203, derived from the CRYSTALS-Kyber submission) is the
NIST-standardised post-quantum KEM. Its security rests on the *module
learning with errors* problem over lattices: roughly, given a matrix of
polynomials $A$ and a vector $t = A s + e$ where $s$ is a secret with small
coefficients and $e$ a small random error, recover $s$. Without the error
term this is linear algebra; with it, the best known algorithms, classical
and quantum alike, take exponential time. Encapsulation encrypts a random
value under $t$ using fresh small randomness, and the shared secret is
hashed from that value. FOKS uses the **ML-KEM-768** parameter set
(security category 3, comparable to AES-192): encapsulation keys are 1184
bytes, ciphertexts 1088 bytes, shared secrets 32 bytes, and key generation
is deterministic from a 64-byte seed $(d, z)$, which lets FOKS derive the
key pair from a device seed (Chapter 3).

References:

- National Institute of Standards and Technology, *Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism Standard*, FIPS 203, 2024, https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.FIPS.203
- J. Bos, L. Ducas, E. Kiltz, T. Lepoint, V. Lyubashevsky, J. M. Schanck, P. Schwabe, G. Seiler, D. Stehlé, *CRYSTALS-Kyber: a CCA-secure module-lattice-based KEM*, IEEE European Symposium on Security and Privacy, 2018, https://eprint.iacr.org/2017/634
- O. Regev, *On Lattices, Learning with Errors, Random Linear Codes, and Cryptography*, Journal of the ACM 56(6), 2009, https://doi.org/10.1145/1568318.1568324

## Hybrid constructions

A *hybrid* key exchange runs a classical and a post-quantum primitive
together and derives the final key from both shared secrets, so that the
result is secure as long as either component is. The essential rule is
that the derivation must hash the public values (ciphertexts or public
keys) along with the secrets, which prevents an attacker from substituting
one component's ciphertext for another that would yield the same combined
key. Chapter 4 shows FOKS's combiner. The same shape is used by the IETF's
hybrid TLS key exchange and permitted by NIST SP 800-56C Rev. 2.

References:

- F. Giacon, F. Heuer, B. Poettering, *KEM Combiners*, PKC 2018, https://eprint.iacr.org/2018/024
- D. Stebila, S. Fluhrer, S. Gueron, *Hybrid key exchange in TLS 1.3*, draft-ietf-tls-hybrid-design, IETF Internet-Draft, https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-tls-hybrid-design/
- E. Barker, L. Chen, R. Davis, *Recommendation for Key-Derivation Methods in Key-Establishment Schemes*, NIST SP 800-56C Rev. 2, 2020, https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-56Cr2

## Key derivation

A *key derivation function* (KDF) turns one secret into others. When the
input is already a uniformly random key, a pseudorandom function such as
HMAC suffices: each distinct label yields an independent-looking key, and
none of them reveals the master. When the input is not uniform (a
Diffie-Hellman shared secret, or a password), an extra step is needed to
condense it first.

**HKDF** (RFC 5869) is the standard two-step KDF: *extract* condenses input
keying material into a uniform pseudorandom key with HMAC under a salt, and
*expand* generates any amount of output from it with HMAC over a context
string and a counter. FOKS does not use HKDF. Its `derive_key` is a single
HMAC-SHA-512/256 over a typed label, which is appropriate because its seeds
are already uniform and it never needs more than one output block
(Chapter 3). The two are mentioned together because the repository's own
guide calls the hierarchy HKDF, and a reader should know the difference.

References:

- H. Krawczyk, P. Eronen, *HMAC-based Extract-and-Expand Key Derivation Function (HKDF)*, RFC 5869, IETF, 2010, https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5869
- H. Krawczyk, *Cryptographic Extraction and Key Derivation: The HKDF Scheme*, CRYPTO 2010, https://eprint.iacr.org/2010/264

## Password hashing

A password has far less entropy than a key, so an attacker who obtains
anything derived from it (a hash, a ciphertext) can try guesses offline.
*Password hashing* functions are deliberately slow and, in modern designs,
*memory-hard*: they require a large amount of memory per evaluation, so
that the parallel hardware attackers use (GPUs, ASICs) gains little over an
ordinary processor. A *salt*, a random value stored alongside, ensures two
users with the same password get different outputs and that precomputed
tables are useless.

**Argon2id** (RFC 9106) is the recommended choice. It takes a memory size,
an iteration count and a parallelism degree as parameters; FOKS's
production values are 64 MiB, 3 iterations and 2 lanes, with a 16-byte
random salt and 64 bytes of output (Chapter 6). The "id" variant mixes the
data-independent memory access of Argon2i (resistant to side-channel
observation) with the data-dependent access of Argon2d (stronger against
time-memory trade-offs).

References:

- A. Biryukov, D. Dinu, D. Khovratovich, S. Josefsson, *Argon2 Memory-Hard Function for Password Hashing and Proof-of-Work Applications*, RFC 9106, IETF, 2021, https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9106
- C. Percival, *Stronger Key Derivation via Sequential Memory-Hard Functions*, BSDCan, 2009, https://www.tarsnap.com/scrypt/scrypt.pdf

## Commitments

A *commitment* lets a party fix a value now and reveal it later, with two
guarantees: the commitment reveals nothing about the value (*hiding*), and
the party cannot later open it to a different value (*binding*). The
simplest practical commitment to a value $v$ is $\text{HMAC}(r, v)$ for a
fresh random key $r$; opening means revealing $r$ and $v$. FOKS uses this
for usernames and device names, which appear in chain links only as
commitments (Chapter 3), and a plain typed hash where the committed value is
itself unguessable (tree locations, removal keys), so that no separate random
key is needed to make the commitment hiding.

References:

- S. Halevi, S. Micali, *Practical and Provably-Secure Commitment Schemes from Collision-Free Hashing*, CRYPTO 1996, https://doi.org/10.1007/3-540-68697-5_16

## Merkle trees

A *Merkle tree* is a tree whose leaves are hashes of data items and whose
every interior node is the hash of its children. The root is a single
digest that commits to every leaf. To prove that a particular leaf is in
the tree, one supplies the sibling hashes along the path from the leaf to
the root, $O(\log n)$ values, and a verifier recomputes the root. Collision
resistance of the hash guarantees that a proof cannot be constructed for a
leaf that is not there. FOKS's server publishes a signed Merkle root over
all chain links, so a client can check that a link it was given is the one
the server committed to, and that the server has not shown different
histories to different clients. Chapter 11 describes the specific tree
(a binary Patricia trie) and Chapter 12 how successive roots are linked.

References:

- R. C. Merkle, *A Digital Signature Based on a Conventional Encryption Function*, CRYPTO 1987, https://doi.org/10.1007/3-540-48184-2_32

## Canonical serialization

Every primitive above operates on bytes. A hash of a data structure is only
meaningful if there is exactly one way to turn that structure into bytes;
otherwise two honest parties may compute different digests of the same
object, or an attacker may find a second encoding of a different object
that hashes the same. A *canonical* encoding is one that admits a single
byte string per value: no optional whitespace, no choice of integer width,
no map-key ordering freedom. FOKS uses a restricted subset of MessagePack
with these rules enforced on both encoding and decoding; Chapter 9 gives
the details and the reasoning.

References:

- S. Furuhashi, *MessagePack specification*, https://github.com/msgpack/msgpack/blob/master/spec.md

## Where to look

- `foks-crypto`: every protocol-level use of the primitives above; the
  crate's top-level module imports name the concrete implementations
  (`sha2`, `sha3`, `hmac`, `ed25519-dalek`, `x25519-dalek`, `p256`,
  `ml-kem`, `crypto_secretbox`, `salsa20`, `argon2`).
- `foks-keystore`: XChaCha20-Poly1305 for local storage.
- `foks-yubi`: ECDSA and ECDH on PIV hardware.
- `foks-snowpack`: canonical serialization.
- The workspace `Cargo.toml` pins the versions of the cryptographic crates.
